name: rv32emu (tiered JIT)
workload: RV32IM guest programs: nbench-derived numeric sort, string sort, bitfield, emfloat, assignment, idea, huffman plus dhrystone, primes and sha512, elapsed time averaged over 200 iterations, rv32emu with tiered JIT versus QEMU.
claimed_speedup: docs say rv32emu with tiered JIT 'outperforms QEMU v9.0.0 across all benchmarks'; the speedup is shown only as a normalised bar chart (docs/jit-bench.png) which reads by eye as about 1.25x (primes, sha512) to about 2.85x (assignment) of QEMU's speed (read from chart image, not stated in text). Reference table on the same page: Threadripper 2990WX Dhrystone 33,365 DMIPS (T2C) vs 2,533 (interpreter), about 13x (derived from page data); CoreMark 13,272 vs 1,835 iterations/s, about 7.2x (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: RV32IM guest toolchain GCC v14.2.0; host build flags of rv32emu and QEMU not stated (DMIPS table lists GCC 14.2 on Threadripper and Clang 18.1 on Ampere eMAG)
hardware: Intel Core i7-11700 at 2.5 GHz, Ubuntu 22.04.1 LTS (QEMU comparison); AMD Threadripper 2990WX and Ampere eMAG (DMIPS/CoreMark table)
tradeoffs: RV32I[MAFC] guest only; an emulator rather than a general language JIT; tiered JIT (modes T1C and T2C in the page's tables); in system mode runs under Linux gain little because SFENCE.VMA flushes discard compiled blocks (page says so).
caveats: Numbers for the QEMU comparison exist only in a PNG chart, values here are eyeballed. The page text calls primes, sha512 and emfloat the biggest gains while the chart shows them among the smallest, so the prose and chart disagree. QEMU flags and the script that produced the chart are not named on the page (tests/interpreter_bench.py is for the libriscv comparison). Baseline is not one of PyPy, LuaJIT, V8, HotSpot. A peer-reviewed VMIL'24 paper is referenced on the repo page but was not opened.
found_via: GitHub topics/jit?l=c (via WebFetch) led to RISC-V JIT emulators; then raw.githubusercontent.com docs/benchmark.md of sysprog21/rv32emu

name: oxtra
workload: Static x86-64 guest programs (a primes calculator and gzip 1.10.7 compressing floating-point CSV files of 132 kB, 526 kB and 13 MB) translated to RISC-V by oxtra and by QEMU; also instruction counts and memory use.
claimed_speedup: Paper text: oxtra is 'up to twice as fast as QEMU' for small inputs (primes below 10,000: oxtra median 20.68 ms vs QEMU 54.71 ms; 132 kB gzip), 'merely 25% faster' gzipping 526 kB and 20% faster with 13 MB; but for primes below 1 million oxtra is 35% slower than QEMU (3685 ms vs 2720 ms medians).
compiler_and_flags: Guests built with a modified musl-gcc fork (no SSE) and statically linked; host flags not stated
hardware: No real RISC-V hardware: everything ran inside system-mode QEMU running Fedora RISC-V (host CPU not stated); instruction counts given as a hardware-independent proxy
tradeoffs: Executes statically linked x86-64 programs only, no SSE support, needs a custom musl fork instead of glibc; RISC-V host only.
caveats: Student project paper (not peer reviewed, documentation/paper/Paper.pdf in the repo). Timings were taken under QEMU system emulation, which the authors say obscures the results. The README claims oxtra 'consistently beats qemu in our toy examples', but the paper shows a 35% loss on the larger primes workload. Benchmark input files ship with the paper source. Baseline is not one of PyPy, LuaJIT, V8, HotSpot.
found_via: WebSearch 'dynamic binary translator OR dynarec faster than QEMU benchmark' surfaced oxtra; then README and documentation/paper/Results.tex via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: Blink
workload: Running x86-64 Linux programs: SSE integer and floating point math benchmarks, and ephemeral programs such as compilers; Blink with its optional JIT versus qemu-x86_64.
claimed_speedup: README: 'Blink goes 2x faster than qemu-x86_64 on some benchmarks, such as SSE integer / floating point math. Blink is also much faster at running ephemeral programs such as compilers.'
tradeoffs: User-mode x86-64-linux emulator, about 221 kB; JIT is optional and only on some host architectures (an interpreter is used on non-JIT hosts).
caveats: First-party one-paragraph claim with no numbers beyond '2x on some benchmarks', no named benchmark suite, QEMU version, flags or CPU. The author's longer write-up (blog) was not reachable. Baseline is not one of PyPy, LuaJIT, V8, HotSpot.
found_via: WebSearch 'dynamic binary translator OR dynarec faster than QEMU' then README of jart/blink via raw.githubusercontent.com and github.com page

name: rv8
workload: RISC-V binaries translated to x86-64 by the rv-jit binary translator (hybrid interpretation and compilation of hot paths, macro-op fusion) versus QEMU.
claimed_speedup: Search-result snippet of the rv8 CARRV 2017 paper (snippet only, paper page blocked): performance 'on average approximately 75% faster than the leading competitor' (QEMU) and within about 30% of native x86-64 on some benchmarks. The README itself has no numbers.
tradeoffs: Targets RISC-V 1.9.1 privileged spec era binaries on x86-64 hosts only; only the Linux syscall proxy ABI is implemented for the JIT simulator (README).
caveats: Snippet only: the paper (rv8: a high performance RISC-V to x86 binary translator, CARRV 2017) could not be opened, so numbers, CPU, flags and QEMU version are unverified; a verifier with paper access could raise the tier (workshop paper). Repo last touched 2018. Baseline is not one of PyPy, LuaJIT, V8, HotSpot.
found_via: WebSearch 'dynamic binary translator OR dynarec faster than QEMU' and github.com/topics/binary-translation; README read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: Instrew
baseline: QEMU and HQEMU (LLVM-based dynamic binary translation)
workload: LLVM-based dynamic binary translator running SPEC-style integer and floating-point benchmarks for x86-64 and RISC-V64 guests on x86-64 hosts, emulation overhead relative to native.
claimed_speedup: Search-result snippet of the VEE 2021 paper 'Efficient LLVM-Based Dynamic Binary Translation' (snippet only, PDF blocked): emulation overhead 53% for Instrew versus 648% for QEMU and 124% for HQEMU; RISC-V to x86-64 integer 76% (Instrew) vs 202% (QEMU), floating point 40% vs 1267% (QEMU). The README has no numbers.
tradeoffs: Needs LLVM at run time (client/server split in the repo); guests x86-64, AArch64, RISC-V64; hosts x86-64 and AArch64 (README).
caveats: Snippet only: numbers come from a search snippet of a peer-reviewed paper (VEE 2021) that could not be opened, so benchmark suite, CPU and flags are unverified; tier C here because nothing was opened, a verifier with the paper may raise it to B. The README cites VEE 2020 as primary paper; the snippet paper may be a later one. Baseline is not one of PyPy, LuaJIT, V8, HotSpot.
found_via: WebSearch 'dynamic binary translator OR dynarec faster than QEMU' returned the VEE 2021 PDF snippet; repo page and README opened on github.com / raw.githubusercontent.com

name: PochiVM (copy-and-patch baseline compiler)
baseline: LLVM JIT at -O0 and higher optimisation levels (compile latency), and interpretation
workload: JIT code generation framework with a copy-and-patch baseline compiler (fastinterp); repo ships a TPC-H mini database backend (mini_db_backend, tpch_data) used to compare compile time and run time with LLVM.
claimed_speedup: From the Copy-and-Patch Compilation paper abstract as shown in a search snippet (snippet only): on TPC-H the compiler generates code two orders of magnitude faster than LLVM -O0 and three orders of magnitude faster than higher LLVM optimisation levels; generated code runs an order of magnitude faster than interpretation and 14% faster than LLVM -O0. The repo README only says the baseline compiler compiles in negligible time 'similar to interpreters' and generates 'better code than LLVM -O0'.
tradeoffs: Generated code is written through a C-like C++ API; research prototype, last touched 2021.
caveats: Snippet only: the paper (Xu and Kjolstad, OOPSLA 2021) could not be opened and the repo has no numbers; attribution of the TPC-H experiment to this repo is inferred from its tpch_data, mini_db_backend and fastinterp directories and the README's mention of copy-and-patch. The WebAssembly numbers in the same abstract belong to the WasmNow repo (already catalogued). Verifier with paper access could raise to B. Baseline is not one of PyPy, LuaJIT, V8, HotSpot.
found_via: github.com/topics/jit-compilation (WebFetch) listed sillycross/PochiVM; WebSearch 'copy-and-patch' gave the abstract snippet

name: RapidUDF
baseline: native scalar C++ (GCC -O2 for the fib comparison; native loops for the vector cases)
workload: LLVM-JIT compiled expressions/UDFs: Fibonacci function, a trigonometric expression over a 4099-element double array, and a Wilson CTR formula over float vectors, JIT with SIMD vectorisation versus the equivalent native C++ function.
claimed_speedup: Vector expression 'acceleration ratio ... reaching 6.09' (207,713 ns scalar JIT / 207,145 ns native vs 33,962 ns vectorised JIT); Wilson CTR 'reaching 10.5' (69,961 ns native vs 6,661 ns vectorised JIT); scalar JIT fib at -O2 roughly on par with native (22,557 ns vs 19,246 ns), and faster than native -O0 (22,547 ns vs 38,933 ns).
compiler_and_flags: optimisation flag O2 for the vectorised tests (compiler for the native baseline not named); LLVM 18+ JIT
hardware: a CPU supporting AVX2 (model not stated)
tradeoffs: Requires LLVM 18+, highway, x86-simd-sort, sleef, abseil and others; C++17; supports a C-like DSL and table API.
caveats: The 6x and 10x wins are SIMD vectorisation (AVX2, SLEEF math) against scalar native code, not a JIT-versus-AOT effect; scalar JIT only matches native. No benchmark source for the quoted numbers was checked and the CPU model is unstated. Baseline is native C++, not one of PyPy, LuaJIT, V8, HotSpot.
found_via: github.com/topics/llvm-jit (WebFetch) listed yinqiwen/rapidudf; README read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: Cinder (Meta CPython fork with method JIT)
workload: Python performance benchmarks with the C++ method-at-a-time Cinder JIT enabled (-X jit), and a typed Static Python version of the Richards benchmark.
claimed_speedup: cinder/3.10 README: the JIT 'can achieve 1.5-4x speed improvements on many Python performance benchmarks'; 'Static Python plus Cinder JIT achieves 18x the performance of stock CPython on a typed version of the Richards benchmark'.
compiler_and_flags: not stated (the same README says its basic build instructions give a binary without PGO/LTO)
stars_or_usage: 3.8k stars; used in production at Meta
tradeoffs: Fork of CPython (default branch now meta/3.14); JIT development has moved to the separate CinderX extension (facebookincubator/cinderx, MIT, 282 stars); Static Python needs type annotations (README).
caveats: Claims sit in the older cinder/3.10 branch README; the current default-branch README has no numbers and says the repo name is historical. No benchmark code, flags, CPU or comparison with PyPy given. 18x applies to a typed, Static-Python-compiled Richards, not ordinary Python. Baseline is not in PyPy, LuaJIT, V8, HotSpot (CPython). Last commit date is for the default branch meta/3.14 (cinder/3.10 branch last commit 2024-06-25).
found_via: WebSearch 'Cinder OR Pyjion OR Eclipse OMR JIT compiler github benchmark speedup over CPython'; README on branch cinder/3.10

name: BeamAsm (Erlang/OTP JIT)
language: C++ (asmjit-based JIT inside the Erlang/OTP runtime)
workload: Erlang/OTP workloads: the estone benchmark suite, JSON encode/decode benchmarks across Erlang and Elixir libraries, and RabbitMQ message throughput, JIT on versus off.
claimed_speedup: PR description: estone score 'about 50% larger'; individual benchmarks 'from a 170% increase (pattern matching) to no change at all (huge messages)'; JSON benchmarks '30% to 130% increase (average at about 70%) in the number of iterations per second'; RabbitMQ handles 30% to 50% more messages per second.
tradeoffs: Load-time template JIT (no tracing or optimising tier), so gains are modest compared with LuaJIT-style tracing JITs; needs a C++17 compiler to build; communication-bound code gains little.
caveats: Numbers are from the PR description of the original merge (September 2020, OTP 24 era); hardware, compiler and flags are not stated on the page; estone and other suites are public but the exact runs are not reproducible from the page. Baseline is the project's own previous interpreter, not one of PyPy, LuaJIT, V8, HotSpot. The entry is the JIT inside a much larger repository.
found_via: WebSearch 'BeamAsm Erlang JIT OTP 24 performance improvement over BEAM interpreter benchmark'; PR page opened on github.com

name: Box64 DynaRec
workload: x86-64 Linux programs run on Arm, RISC-V and LoongArch hosts, dynamic recompiler (DynaRec) versus the project's own interpreter.
claimed_speedup: README: 'With DynaRec for Arm, RISC-V and LoongArch platforms, Box64 achieves a speed boost 5-10x faster than the interpreter alone.'
tradeoffs: User-mode x86-64 Linux emulator that wraps native system libraries; Wine/Proton support; JIT only on the three listed host architectures.
caveats: Baseline is the project's own interpreter, not an independent incumbent; no workload, CPU or flags named; the linked performance analysis (box86.org blog) and the EuroSys 2026 paper cited by the repo were not reachable, so no comparison with QEMU or FEX was verified.
found_via: WebSearch 'dynamic binary translator OR dynarec faster than QEMU' listed Box64; README and repo page opened

name: Easy::jit
baseline: the same kernel compiled ahead of time (non-specialised) with clang
workload: Runtime specialisation of C++ functions by embedding their LLVM IR in the binary and recompiling with LLVM ORC when argument values are known: an image convolution kernel and a quicksort kernel.
claimed_speedup: Search-result snippet of the Quarkslab blog post (snippet only, blog not opened): the convolution kernel runs roughly 4.5x faster and the quicksort kernel around 2x faster than the original version. The repo README has no numbers.
tradeoffs: Compiler-assisted: needs a Clang/LLVM pass plugin and an LLVM runtime library; functions must be annotated; compile cost paid at run time, with a cache to avoid recompiling.
caveats: Snippet only; the numbers come from the Quarkslab blog (EuroLLVM'18 / FOSDEM'18 era) and could not be verified. benchmark/benchmark.cpp (Google Benchmark) exists in the repo but no results are checked in. Baseline is AOT code of the same function, not one of PyPy, LuaJIT, V8, HotSpot. Last commit 2021.
found_via: WebSearch 'github C++ expression JIT OR query compilation library benchmark faster than LLVM' and github.com/topics/jit?l=c++

name: HHVM
workload: Server-side Hack (formerly PHP) programs executed by a JIT virtual machine.
claimed_speedup: no numbers: README says HHVM 'uses a just-in-time (JIT) compilation approach to achieve superior performance'; baseline is not named on the page.
license: PHP-3.01 AND Zend-2.0 (core); MIT (Hack typechecker and Hack Standard Library)
tradeoffs: Runs Hack (and, historically, PHP 5/7 code) only; HHVM now targets Hack and PHP support was dropped in later releases (not verified on the pages opened), so any PHP comparison is historical; needs a webserver such as Proxygen or FastCGI.
caveats: Tier D, included only because the project is widely referenced. The baseline (PHP) is inferred, not stated on the page; the Zend-2.0 licence part is not OSI-approved, hence usability mixed. Earlier PHP-versus-HHVM numbers lived on blogs and the docs site, which were not reachable.
found_via: Checked as a known JIT VM while browsing github.com/topics and READMEs (raw.githubusercontent.com facebook/hhvm README.md)
